key_terms.term: Distributed parameters R, L, G, C
key_terms.meaning: Resistance, inductance, conductance and capacitance per metre of line; they replace lumped values when the line is longer than a fraction of a wavelength.
∂v/∂z = −Ri − L ∂i/∂t and ∂i/∂z = −Gv − C ∂v/∂t, the two coupled equations that describe voltage and current along a line.
Z₀ = √((R + jωL)/(G + jωC)) Ω; for a lossless line it reduces to √(L/C).
γ = α + jβ = √((R + jωL)(G + jωC)); α in Np/m sets loss, β in rad/m sets phase.
A line with R/L = G/C, so α is flat and vp = 1/√(LC) is the same for all frequencies and the pulse shape is preserved.
vp = ω/β = λf, the speed at which a single frequency's phase travels down the line.
Γ = (Z_L − Z₀)/(Z_L + Z₀), a complex number giving the amplitude and phase of the wave sent back by the load.
Voltage standing wave ratio S = (1 + |Γ|)/(1 − |Γ|), the ratio of maximum to minimum voltage on a mismatched line.
Return loss = −20 log₁₀|Γ| dB; a large value means little power comes back.
The fixed pattern of voltage maxima and minima produced when a forward and a reflected wave of the same frequency add.
Z_in = Z₀(Z_L + jZ₀ tan βl)/(Z₀ + jZ_L tan βl), the impedance seen at distance l from the load.
Line length measured in radians or degrees, βl = 2πl/λ; it decides how a load is transformed.
A λ/4 section of impedance Z₀′ = √(Z₀ Z_L) that turns a real load into a match at one frequency.
A shorted or open line section of length ls placed in parallel or series to cancel the load reactance so the input looks like Z₀.
A polar plot of Γ on which normalized impedance and admittance circles turn matching into a ruler-and-compass construction.
The permittivity a printed line behaves as if it had, because its field is split between substrate and air.
The lowest frequency at which a waveguide mode propagates; below fc the wave decays and carries no real power.
λg = 2π/β = λ₀/√(1 − (fc/f)²), the spacing between phase fronts inside the guide.
The lowest-order rectangular-waveguide mode, with fc = c/(2a) for broad wall a; the usual working mode.
Q = ω₀ × (energy stored)/(power lost) = f₀/BW; it sets how sharp a resonator's response is.

takeaways: A transmission line is described completely by four per-metre quantities, and from them Z₀, α, β and vp follow.
When R/L equals G/C the line is distortionless, so attenuation is flat and a pulse keeps its shape.
Any load mismatch sends back a wave; Γ measures it, S and return loss report it, and both are read directly from |Γ|.
Input impedance depends on load and electrical length, so a short looks like an inductor, an open like a capacitor, and a λ/2 section repeats the load.
A quarter-wave transformer matches a real load only near one frequency, while a stub cancels reactance at a chosen point on the line.
The Smith chart is just the Γ plane with impedance circles drawn on it, so every matching step is a rotation and a circle crossing.
Printed lines such as microstrip and stripline trade compactness and easy fabrication against loss and radiation, with ε_eff setting Z₀ and λ.
A hollow waveguide passes a mode only above its cutoff, and the mode indices plus the metal dimensions fix fc, λg and vp.
A resonator's Q ties stored energy to loss; higher Q means a narrower bandwidth and a longer ring-down time.
Matching buys power transfer and low reflection, but every matching network has a finite bandwidth that must be checked.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to combine a clean derivation of the line equations with a numerical impedance, matching or waveguide calculation, and to justify the choice between coax, printed line and waveguide for a given band.

bank.q: Define the distributed parameters of a transmission line and derive the telegrapher's equations from a short element of length Δz. Solve them for a sinusoidal source to obtain Z₀ and γ.
outline: Draw the element with series RΔz, LΔz and shunt GΔz, CΔz
Apply KVL and KVL, divide by Δz, let Δz → 0
Write the two first-order equations; differentiate to get second-order wave equations
Assume V = V₀e^(−γz) and state γ = α + jβ = √((R + jωL)(G + jωC))
State Z₀ = √((R + jωL)/(G + jωC)) and the lossless limits √(L/C) and β = ω√(LC)
Give units: R, L, G, C per metre; α in Np/m, β in rad/m, Z₀ in ohms

bank.q: What is waveform distortion on a line? Derive the condition for a distortionless line and explain how loading coils approximate it.
outline: Distortion = different frequencies attenuated differently and travelling at different speeds, so a pulse spreads
α = Re(γ) depends on ω in general; β/ω also varies, giving dispersion
Distortionless condition R/L = G/C
Then α = √(RG) independent of ω and vp = 1/√(LC) independent of ω
Loading adds series inductance L to bring R/L down towards G/C
Remark that this works for audio pairs, not for microwave lines

bank.q: Define reflection coefficient, VSWR and return loss for a line terminated in Z_L. Derive the relations between them and state the values for open, short and matched loads.
outline: Γ = (Z_L − Z₀)/(Z_L + Z₀), generally complex
|Γ| ≤ 1; Γ = +1 open, −1 short, 0 matched
Voltage on line is V⁺(e^(−jβl) + Γe^(+jβl)); maxima and minima spaced λ/2 apart
Return loss = −20 log|Γ| dB; matched gives infinite return loss
Power delivered to load = incident power × (1 − |Γ|²)

bank.q: Explain TE and TM modes in a rectangular waveguide. Derive the cutoff frequency of the TE₁₀ mode and explain why it is called the dominant mode.
outline: TE: E_z = 0, H_z ≠ 0; TM: H_z = 0, E_z ≠ 0; TEM cannot exist in a single-conductor hollow guide
Boundary conditions give kc² = (mπ/a)² + (nπ/b)²
TE₁₀ has the lowest fc = c/2a for a > b
Below fc, γ is real, the wave decays as e^(−αz), no real power flows
Sketch the field pattern and the surface current on the broad wall

bank.q: A 50 Ω lossless line of length 0.3λ is terminated in Z_L = 100 + j50 Ω. Calculate the reflection coefficient at the load, the VSWR, and the input impedance.
outline: Γ_L = (Z_L − Z₀)/(Z_L + Z₀), compute magnitude and angle in complex form
|Γ| from the result; S = (1 + |Γ|)/(1 − |Γ|)
βl = 2π × 0.3 = 0.6π rad, tan βl evaluated correctly
Use Z_in = Z₀(Z_L + jZ₀ tan βl)/(Z₀ + jZ_L tan βl)
Alternatively rotate Γ_L by −2βl and convert back
State units (Ω) and that the answer is complex

bank.q: Design a quarter-wave transformer to match a 200 Ω resistive load to a 50 Ω line at 2 GHz on an air-spaced line. Find the section impedance and its physical length, and state the bandwidth limitation.
outline: l = λ/4 with λ = c/f = 0.15 m, so l = 37.5 mm
Transformer works exactly at f₀ only; reflection grows away from f₀
Bandwidth widens for smaller impedance ratio
Mention that the load must be real; otherwise a stub must first cancel reactance

bank.q: A 50 Ω line feeds a load of 25 + j40 Ω at 1 GHz. Using the Smith chart, find the position and length of a single short-circuited shunt stub that matches the line.
outline: Normalize z_L = 0.5 + j0.8 and plot it
Rotate towards the generator to the g = 1 circle (or the 1 + jb circle) and read the distance d in wavelengths
Read the susceptance b at that point and convert to admittance
Stub susceptance must be −b; locate the short (y = ∞) and move along the outer circle
Read stub length ls in wavelengths, convert to metres with λ = c/f
Note the two possible solutions and the physical realizability check

bank.q: A microstrip line is built on a 0.8 mm thick substrate with εr = 4.4 and copper strip width 1.5 mm. Explain the steps to find Z₀, ε_eff and the guided wavelength at 5 GHz, and state why closed-form formulas are only approximate.
outline: Compute W/h = 1.875; use a microstrip synthesis/analysis formula or a chart
ε_eff = (εr + 1)/2 + (εr − 1)/2 × 1/√(1 + 12h/W), giving a value between 1 and εr
Z₀ falls as W/h rises and as ε_eff rises
λg = λ₀/√ε_eff, with λ₀ = 60 mm at 5 GHz
Formulas are curve fits to quasi-static solutions; fringing fields, dispersion and finite strip thickness are ignored
Confirm with a field solver or measurement

bank.q: A rectangular cavity resonator is 30 mm × 15 mm × 20 mm and operates in the TE₁₀₁ mode. Outline the calculation of its resonant frequency and its unloaded Q if the surface resistance is known.
outline: Resonant frequency f = (c/2)√((m/a)² + (p/d)²) for TE₁₀ₚ with length d
Substitute a = 30 mm, d = 20 mm, p = 1 and give f in GHz
Q = ω₀ × stored energy / power lost; copper loss ∝ Rs
State that Q falls as Rs rises (higher frequency, rougher surface)
Loaded Q includes external coupling and is lower than unloaded Q
Bandwidth BW = f₀/Q_L

bank.q: Compare microstrip, stripline and coplanar waveguide for a 10 GHz front end. Discuss loss, radiation, dispersion, fabrication and the ease of mounting shunt components.
outline: Field picture of each: microstrip half-air half-dielectric, stripline fully buried, CPW both conductors on one face
ε_eff of microstrip < εr, so it radiates at bends and has higher loss; stripline is shielded and non-dispersive
CPW keeps ground close, so shunt parts mount without vias; microstrip needs vias
Fabrication: all are etched on PCB or thin film; stripline needs bonding of layers
Dispersion and higher-order modes set an upper frequency for each
Choose: microstrip for cheap mixed-signal boards, stripline for shielded low-loss runs, CPW for mm-wave MMICs

bank.q: Explain how the Smith chart is constructed from the reflection-coefficient plane, and show how line rotation, VSWR and matching appear on it.
outline: Γ = |Γ|e^(jθ); the chart is the unit circle of |Γ| ≤ 1
Substitute Γ = (z − 1)/(z + 1) to get constant-r and constant-x circles
Constant r circles centred on the real axis, constant x arcs from the right-hand point
Lossless line movement = clockwise rotation by 2βl at constant |Γ|, half a turn per λ/2
VSWR = value of r at the positive real-axis crossing of the |Γ| circle
Matching: move to g = 1, then add a stub of the right susceptance
Limits: the chart is lossless and single frequency; lossy lines spiral inwards

bank.q: Discuss the high-frequency effects that make the simple R, L, G, C model break down, and explain how they change the choice of matching method and its bandwidth.
outline: Skin effect raises R with √f; proximity effect adds more
Dielectric loss makes G rise with frequency; tan δ of the substrate
Dispersion: ε_eff and Z₀ vary with frequency on microstrip
Radiation and surface waves at higher frequencies
Component parasitics: lead inductance, pad capacitance, so lumped matching fails above a few GHz
Distributed matching (stubs, tapers) preferred; narrowband vs broadband trade-off; Bode–Fano limit links match quality and bandwidth
Measure with a VNA and S-parameters rather than assuming the model

bank.q: A 28 GHz link must carry 1 W. Recommend a transmission medium and a matching approach, justifying the choice against waveguide, coaxial line and printed microstrip.
outline: Waveguide: lowest loss per metre at mm-wave, high power handling, bulky, cut off below fc
Coax: convenient up to about 20 GHz; losses and connector repeatability hurt at 28 GHz
Microstrip: compact, integrates with the radio chip, but loss, radiation and tight tolerance at 28 GHz
Compare attenuation in dB/m, power handling, size and cost
Matching: waveguide iris or stub for the antenna feed, printed stub or taper on the board
Note bandwidth required by 1 W and linearity, plus mechanical alignment tolerance

glossary.def: A pair of conductors, or a conductor over a ground plane, that guides a wave from source to load.
Per-metre values R, L, G and C that describe a line whose length is comparable with a wavelength.
The coupled first-order equations for voltage and current along a line.
The ratio of forward voltage to forward current on a line, Z₀ = √((R + jωL)/(G + jωC)).
γ = α + jβ, the complex number giving attenuation and phase change per metre.
α, the real part of γ, in nepers per metre; it sets how fast the wave shrinks.
β, the imaginary part of γ, in radians per metre; it sets wavelength along the line.
The speed at which one frequency's phase travels, vp = ω/β.
The speed at which the envelope of a modulated signal travels, vg = dω/dβ.
A line with R/L = G/C, so all frequencies are attenuated equally and travel at the same speed.
Γ = (Z_L − Z₀)/(Z_L + Z₀), the complex ratio of reflected to incident voltage at the load.
A fixed pattern of voltage maxima and minima formed by forward and reflected waves.
Voltage standing wave ratio, S = (1 + |Γ|)/(1 − |Γ|), between 1 and infinity.
−20 log₁₀|Γ| in dB; the larger the value, the better the match.
Line length expressed as βl in radians or as a fraction of a wavelength.
The impedance seen looking into a line at a given distance from the load.
A short length of line, open or shorted, placed in shunt or series to cancel reactance.
A λ/4 line of impedance √(Z₀Z_L) that matches a real load to a line at one frequency.
A polar chart of reflection coefficient on which normalized impedance and admittance are plotted.
A printed strip on one side of a dielectric slab with a ground plane on the other.
A printed strip buried between two ground planes in a dielectric.
A centre strip with ground strips on the same face of the substrate.
The permittivity a printed line behaves as if it had when its field is partly in air.
The frequency below which a waveguide mode cannot propagate.
The distance between phase fronts inside a waveguide, λg = λ₀/√(1 − (fc/f)²).
Q = ω₀ × stored energy ÷ lost power, which fixes a resonator's bandwidth.
